hook.question: You have one meeting room and a pile of meeting requests for today. Which request do you say yes to first, if you want to fit in as many as you can?
paragraphs: Say the day has four requests: 8–12, 9–10, 10–11 and 11–12. The one that starts first (8–12) sounds natural to grab, but it fills the whole morning and leaves room for nothing else. You attend one meeting.

Now try one rule instead: always say yes to the request that ends soonest, as long as it doesn't clash with what you've already booked. That books 9–10, then 10–11, then 11–12. Three meetings, from a rule you can say in one breath.
hook.aha: Finishing early leaves the most room for everything after it. You can even prove that no other first pick does better: swap the first meeting of any plan for the earliest-ending one and nothing later gets bumped. That proof is what makes a greedy rule safe. Without it, a rule that sounds sensible can quietly fail.

metaphor: Packing your day, you keep asking one question: of the things left, which one frees me up soonest? You say yes to that one, and you never reopen the decision.
Each yes leaves as much of the day as possible for whatever is still to come.
mentalModel.click: Take the pick that leaves the most room, never look back, and be able to argue that no other pick could have done better.

glossary.definition: The pick that looks best right now, made without looking ahead and never undone. In scheduling it is the interval that ends earliest.
The best option at a single step, judged only by what you can see right now.
The best answer for the whole problem. Greedy is only correct when a string of local optima adds up to this.
The proof that makes greedy safe: take any best answer, swap its first pick for the greedy pick, and show it is still best.
A small input where the greedy rule gives a worse answer than the best one. A single counterexample is enough to throw the rule out.
The field you sort by so the best pick comes first. For meetings it is the end time, not the start time or the length.
Two intervals share some time. Touching at one moment (one ends at 3, the next starts at 3) does not count.
In Jump Game, the farthest index any jump so far can land on. It only ever grows.

mentalModel.definition: A greedy algorithm builds an answer one step at a time, always taking the choice that looks best right now and never revisiting it. It is correct only when two things hold: some best answer begins with that choice (the greedy-choice property, usually shown with an exchange argument), and what remains after the choice is a smaller copy of the same problem. When a choice can block a better combination later, greedy fails. With coins 1, 3 and 4 and an amount of 6, taking the biggest coin first gives 4 + 1 + 1 = 3 coins, but 3 + 3 needs only 2. Those problems need dynamic programming.

tracks.label: Jump game: how far can you reach?

useWhen: The data is intervals or tasks with start and end times, and you have to pick or schedule as many as possible.
The statement asks for a minimum or maximum count, like the most meetings, the fewest arrows or the fewest removals, and sorting by one field makes the best pick obvious.
You can say why taking the best-looking option now can never hurt later, for example because you could swap it into any other plan.
You scan once, keeping a single running number such as the farthest reach or the last end, and each step needs only that number.
notWhen: A choice now can block a better combination later, like coins 1, 3, 4 for amount 6. Greedy gives 3 coins where 2 is possible, so use dynamic-programming.
You must count the number of ways or list every solution. One confident pass can't do that; reach for recursion or dynamic-programming.
You can't explain why the pick is safe, and a small counterexample breaks it. Don't trust the rule until you have the argument.

quiz.problem: You have a list of meetings [start, end] and one room. Find the largest number of meetings you can attend with no overlap.
quiz.explanation: Sort by end time and keep every meeting that starts at or after the last kept one ends. Finishing earliest leaves the most room, and an exchange argument proves no other first pick is better.

quiz.problem: Given coins [1, 3, 4] and an amount of 6, find the fewest coins that add up to it.
quiz.explanation: Taking the biggest coin first gives 4 + 1 + 1 = 3 coins, but 3 + 3 uses only 2. The big pick blocks a better combination, so greedy fails. Build the best answer for every amount from 1 up: that is dynamic programming.

quiz.problem: Numbers keep arriving in a stream. After each one, report the 3rd largest number seen so far.
quiz.explanation: You repeatedly need the smallest of the current top 3 and must swap numbers in and out. A min-heap of size 3 does that in O(log k) per number, where k = 3.

quiz.problem: nums[i] is how far you can jump from index i. Starting at index 0, decide whether you can reach the last index.
quiz.explanation: Track the farthest index you can reach so far. If the next index is past it you are stuck; otherwise stretch the reach. One pass, no search, and you can show the reach never needs to shrink.

quiz.problem: Given a string, find the length of the longest substring that has no repeating characters.
quiz.explanation: The answer is a contiguous stretch whose condition (no repeats) can break and be repaired at its left edge. That is a window growing on the right and shrinking on the left, with no pick to defend.

pseudocode.text: sort intervals by end, earliest first
for each (start, end) in the sorted list:

notes: Why sort by end? Sort by start and one long meeting like 0–10 blocks three short ones. Sort by shortest first and a short 3–5 sitting between 1–4 and 4–8 blocks both, though those two fit together. Only the earliest end always leaves the most room.
Touching is fine: if one interval ends at 3 and the next starts at 3, they don't overlap. That is why the test is start >= last_end, not start > last_end.

The exchange argument in four lines: take any best schedule, swap its first interval for the earliest-ending one, and note that it ends no later, so everything after it still fits. The schedule is no worse, so some best schedule starts with the greedy pick. Repeat for what remains.
Sorting costs O(n log n) and the sweep is a single O(n) pass, so the sort dominates. Beyond the sort you keep only two numbers: last_end and removed.

Greedy is not a default; it is a claim you have to defend. Always-take-the-biggest-coin works for coins like 1, 5, 10, 25, but with coins [1, 3, 4] and amount 6 it picks 4 + 1 + 1 = 3 coins while 3 + 3 = 2 is best. When a choice can block a better combination later, use dynamic-programming.

examples.title: Jump Game
examples.problem: Each number in nums is the farthest you can jump from that index. Starting at index 0, return true if you can reach the last index, otherwise false.
approach: Track reach, the farthest index any jump so far can land on. It starts at 0.
Index 0 lets you jump 3, so reach = 3. Indexes 1 and 2 also land on 3 (1 + 2 and 2 + 1), and index 3 jumps 0, so reach stays 3.
Index 4 is past reach: no jump can land there. You are stuck before the end, so the answer is false.
If reach ever covers the last index you can stop early, because the answer is then true.

examples.title: Non-overlapping Intervals
examples.problem: Given intervals where intervals[i] = [start, end], return the minimum number of intervals to remove so that the rest do not overlap. Intervals that only touch at an endpoint do not overlap.
approach: Removing the fewest means keeping the most, so always keep the interval that ends earliest.
Sort by end: [1,2], [2,3], [1,3], [3,4]. Keep [1,2] (last end = 2). [2,3] starts at 2, which only touches, so keep it (last end = 3).
[1,3] starts at 1, before 3, so it overlaps: drop it. [3,4] starts at 3, so keep it.

examples.title: Jump Game II
examples.problem: Same jumps as Jump Game, but you can always reach the last index. Return the minimum number of jumps needed to get there.
approach: Think in rounds. cur_end is the farthest index the jumps used so far can reach, and farthest is how far one more jump could take you.
Index 0: farthest = 2. You are at cur_end (0), so you must jump: jumps = 1 and cur_end = 2.
Index 1 stretches farthest to 4 (1 + 3). Index 2 is the end of this round (cur_end = 2), so jump again: jumps = 2 and cur_end = 4, the last index.
Stop before the last index, since there is nothing to jump from there. The answer is 2.

conceptQuiz.question: You want the most non-overlapping meetings. Which sort order makes the greedy pick safe?
conceptQuiz.explanation: Earliest end leaves the most room for what follows. Start-first fails on 0–10 in front of three short meetings, and shortest-first fails on 3–5 sitting between 1–4 and 4–8.

conceptQuiz.question: Coins are [1, 3, 4] and the amount is 6. What does "always take the biggest coin that fits" give, and what is the best possible?
options: Greedy gives 2 coins and the best is 3.
Greedy and the best both give 3 coins.
Greedy gives 2 coins, which is also the best.
Greedy gives 3 coins (4 + 1 + 1), but 2 coins (3 + 3) is the best.
conceptQuiz.explanation: Taking the 4 first leaves 2, which costs two 1s. One counterexample is enough to show greedy fails for this coin set, so you would use dynamic programming.

conceptQuiz.question: What does an exchange argument show?
options: Swapping the greedy pick into the first spot of any best answer never makes it worse, so some best answer uses it.
That the algorithm runs in O(n log n).
That the input must be sorted first.
That every other pick is wrong.
conceptQuiz.explanation: It is a proof, not a speed claim. If you can swap your pick into any best answer without losing anything, committing to that pick can't cost you the best answer.

conceptQuiz.question: You find a small input where your greedy rule gives a worse answer than the best. What should you do?
options: Keep the rule: real tests are usually friendlier.
Change the rule or switch approach, for example to dynamic programming.
Add a special case for that one input.
conceptQuiz.explanation: A single counterexample disproves the rule. Patching one input leaves the same flaw on the next, so look for a different pick or let dynamic programming try every option.

conceptQuiz.question: For nums = [1, 0, 2] in Jump Game, what does the reach scan conclude?
options: True: index 2 can jump 2, which is plenty.
True: reach grows to 3 at index 2.
False: reach stays at 1, so index 2 is out of reach before its jump counts.
False: index 0 can't jump at all.
conceptQuiz.explanation: Index 0 lets you jump 1, so reach = 1. Index 1 jumps 0, so reach stays 1. Index 2 is past reach, so you never get to stand on it.

practice.title: Assign Cookies
practice.insight: Sort children by greed and cookies by size, then give each child the smallest cookie that still satisfies them.

practice.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock II
practice.insight: You may trade every day. Think about each rise from one day to the next on its own, rather than hunting for one big buy and sell.

practice.title: Gas Station
practice.insight: If total gas is less than total cost, no start works. Otherwise, when your tank first goes negative, every station up to there is a bad start.

practice.title: Partition Labels
practice.insight: Record the last position of every letter. Keep stretching the current part to cover those last positions, and cut when i catches up.

practice.title: Task Scheduler
practice.insight: The most frequent task forces the gaps. Lay it out first, then check whether the other tasks can fill the gaps or leave idle slots.

practice.title: Two City Scheduling
practice.insight: Look at costA − costB for each person: it says how much more they prefer one city. Sort by that gap.

practice.title: Queue Reconstruction by Height
practice.insight: Place people from tallest to shortest, so a shorter person never changes the count of someone already placed.

practice.title: Candy
practice.insight: Satisfy the left-neighbour rule in one pass and the right-neighbour rule in another, then keep the larger requirement for each child.

practice.title: Merge Intervals
practice.insight: Sort by start so overlaps become neighbours. Then keep stretching the last output interval while the next one starts at or before its end.

practice.title: Insert Interval
practice.insight: The list is already sorted. Copy everything that ends before the new one, merge everything that overlaps it, then copy the rest.

overview: Explain why finishing earliest leaves the most room for later picks.
Trace the earliest-end rule through a list of meetings, keeping or dropping each.
Trace the farthest-reach rule through the jump game, one index at a time.
Spot when a locally best pick is unsafe and dynamic programming is needed.
Implement the sort-then-scan template for interval scheduling in O(n log n).
